standard: UK Cyber Security Council SPCC v4.2 with the Incident Response contextualisation (v2)

profile.name: Danny Howett
profile.conf: Client names, systems, threat actor details and some figures have been anonymised or omitted because of legal, contractual and security obligations. Each example accurately reflects my own responsibilities, the work I delegated, the authority I worked under, the decisions I made and the outcomes achieved. My referees can verify the substance of these claims.

evidence.title: Ransomware response for a multinational telecommunications provider
evidence.scale: Large, interconnected network spanning multiple countries, with several thousand staff
evidence.situation: A multinational telecommunications provider suffered a double-extortion ransomware attack in which servers were encrypted across several countries and data was exfiltrated. The attack disrupted telephony services for some customers and took critical internal systems offline. The client's cyber insurer referred the engagement to my firm, so there was no prior relationship with, or knowledge of, the environment. Stakeholders included the client's executive, IT and legal teams, its data protection officer, the cyber insurer and external legal counsel.
evidence.task: The immediate priority was to restore telephony services for affected customers, followed by critical and then wider business services. In parallel, regulators in several jurisdictions, each with different obligations, required timely updates. I also led the threat actor engagement workstream, initially to establish whether data had been exfiltrated and to understand the attackers' demands.
evidence.action:
In the initial hours, stakeholders were unable to confirm whether the network was segmented. I recommended immediate network isolation to contain the attack, despite incomplete visibility of the environment. Isolation carried significant business disruption, but further encryption would have delayed recovery by weeks and extended customer impact, so I judged it the lower risk.

I structured the response around the NIST SP 800-61r3 incident response lifecycle and led an investigation team of five to ten people, initially divided broadly equally between containment and the collection of IOCs and evidence of persistence, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. I agreed a reporting cadence that kept the client informed while protecting the team's investigative capacity, with all updates provided under legal privilege. I supported the client's regulatory notifications, including updates to the ICO under the UK GDPR, and provided the insurer with a projected run rate at the outset and weekly cost reports for approval.

The initial phase focused on restoring customer-facing services and preventing further spread. Working with the client's IT and infrastructure teams, I identified the hosts affecting service availability, triaged them and assessed backup viability, restoring only from backups that triage had verified as clean. Containment included isolating affected network segments, preparing EDR tooling for deployment, and triaging high-value hosts to identify IOCs and remove persistent access, such as C2 channels and backdoors.

Once critical services were restored, the engagement moved to root cause analysis, validation of the attacker's data theft claims and eradication of persistence. The team built an isolated recovery environment in which hosts declared clean were placed in a DMZ under EDR monitoring and threat hunting at scale, and returned to production only once fully validated. The engagement lasted approximately three months.
evidence.result: The team restored customer-facing services within 48 hours, most within 24 to 36 hours, and the majority of critical services, including support and account management functions, within a week. Full restoration and validation of the environment was confirmed after approximately three months. A decryption tool accelerated recovery; engagement with the threat actor was necessary because certain key business systems could not otherwise be recovered without significant rebuild effort, and the engagement secured a substantial reduction in the original demand. All sanctions due diligence, including OFSI and OFAC screening, was completed and passed, and the associated risks were fully explained to the board. The client's infrastructure team subsequently confirmed that the network was not fully segmented: without isolation, further systems would have been encrypted and additional services affected.
evidence.followup: I led a post-incident review with key IT and executive stakeholders, which recorded what had worked well and identified several improvement actions, each with a named owner. The run rate tracked closely to projection, with the insurer approving costs weekly. Despite having no prior relationship with my firm, the client went on to invest a six-figure sum in proactive and readiness services, alongside a multi-year managed service covering a range of offensive and defensive capabilities.

evidence.title: Forensic examination in support of civil litigation (intellectual property theft)
evidence.scale: Forensic examination of more than 15 devices and accounts
evidence.situation: The client, a manufacturing company, was pursuing civil proceedings against a former employee who had left to establish a competing business in Malaysia using lower-cost production tooling and labour. The company alleged that he had taken a significant volume of its intellectual property.
evidence.task: I was instructed to examine a range of the former employee's devices and accounts, including laptops, mobile phones, external media, cloud storage and email, the latter under the authority of a court order, to determine whether evidence supported the company's allegations.
evidence.action: I conducted the examination in accordance with the four ACPO principles for digital evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012, ensuring that original evidence remained unaltered and that an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. I maintained contemporaneous notes and photographic records throughout. All devices were received powered off; I photographed each item, acquired a physical forensic image, verified each acquisition by hash, and preserved chain of custody and evidential integrity at every stage. Analysis was undertaken on a dedicated, forensically clean workstation using commercial forensic tools in which I am trained and experienced.
evidence.result: My examination established that the company's intellectual property had been taken without authority. Although most devices showed no relevant activity, an iCloud backup on a Mac device contained a messaging application conversation between the former employee and others that provided compelling evidence of the allegation, together with web searches relating to data destruction and the removal of search history. Analysis of that conversation identified a second messaging application, which the former employee had described as "not on their radar", containing evidence of extensive data theft.
evidence.followup: I set out my findings in an affidavit and subsequently gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court. The company was successful in its claim.

evidence.title: Incident response plan and runbook design for a managed service client
evidence.scale: Incident response plan and six runbooks
evidence.situation: My firm assumed responsibility for a range of managed services for a client, including DFIR, previously provided by a third party. During knowledge transfer I identified that the existing incident response plan (IRP) was outdated and that no scenario-specific runbooks existed, leaving a material gap in the client's preparedness.
evidence.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a new IRP and runbooks for the client's most likely and highest-impact scenarios, selected using threat intelligence relevant to its sector and geography and validated with the client.
evidence.action: I aligned the IRP to the incident response lifecycle in NIST SP 800-61r3 and to ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications, communication channels and escalation routes. For each runbook I documented step-by-step procedures for detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. I tested every command and query, including KQL queries, in the client's live environment to confirm that each was functional and appropriate.
evidence.result: The client formally approved the IRP and six validated runbooks and adopted them as the standard for its SOC and incident response teams. An annual review cycle, with additional reviews triggered by significant vendor or network changes, keeps them current.
evidence.followup: The runbooks have since been used in live incidents. After each incident, a lessons-learned review gathers feedback from senior stakeholders and key responders, and the findings are incorporated into the next version.

evidence.title: Executive tabletop exercise for a global news organisation
evidence.scale: C-suite tabletop exercise with attendees from London, Germany and Hong Kong
evidence.situation: The client, a global news organisation, engaged us following an incident in which malware on a personal (BYOD) device reached its corporate network. Although the attack was unsuccessful and the underlying vulnerabilities had been remediated, unclear decision-making had slowed the response, and the client wished to test its readiness and decision-making. Executives from London, Germany and Hong Kong attended in person, alongside key IT stakeholders from across the business.
evidence.task: I was responsible for designing and facilitating a tabletop exercise to assess the organisation's readiness for a significant malware incident, test its incident response plan and identify gaps in decision-making and coordination. I had three to four weeks to prepare, supported by two researchers.
evidence.action:
I began with scoping sessions with the IT team to understand their bespoke and commercial tooling, the circumstances of the near miss and the objectives for the exercise. I built the scenario around the client's own in-house and proprietary systems, so that non-technical attendees would recognise them, and developed the real incident into a significant malware attack involving data exfiltration and extortion, informed by current threat actor tactics. I produced a delegate briefing pack and ran two internal rehearsals, refining injects that were sound in theory but did not work in practice.

Timed injects tested strategic and technical decision-making, business impact and prioritisation, regulatory notification, ransom payment and sanctions considerations, and media and public relations handling. I facilitated the discussion while my team recorded decisions in real time. I challenged a key assumption by asking how decisions would be made if the named decision-makers were unavailable: the playbook assigned critical business decisions to individuals with no deputies, which prompted a discussion of delegated authority for time-critical decisions. Following the exercise, I gathered feedback and produced a post-exercise report setting out findings and recommendations.
evidence.result: Client feedback was positive, and the exercise identified several gaps in the organisation's response capability.
evidence.followup: Around two weeks later I met the IT team that had commissioned the exercise. Having gathered feedback from attendees, they agreed several practical improvements for immediate implementation and a roadmap for further changes, including regular practical testing of procedures that had previously existed only in documentation, such as backup retrieval and restoration. I monitor progress through monthly calls with the client.

evidence.title: Career pathways and SOC-to-DFIR mentoring
evidence.scale: Six career frameworks for the team, plus one-to-one mentoring
evidence.situation: In my current role, I volunteered to support the team's learning and development function.
evidence.task: To develop a set of career pathways for the team, and to mentor a junior colleague transitioning from a SOC role into DFIR.
evidence.action: I developed six career frameworks aligned to SFIA 9: SOC, DFIR, a SOC-to-DFIR transition pathway, GRC, offensive security, and security advisory and consulting. Each defines grades mapped to SFIA levels of responsibility and skills, with recommended certifications, relevant professional bodies (including CIISec, the UK Cyber Security Council, CREST and BCS), a gap analysis and curated learning resources. The SOC-to-DFIR pathway maps a SOC analyst's existing skills to their DFIR equivalents and identifies the gaps to close. I also mentor a junior colleague through this transition.
evidence.result: All six frameworks are complete. My mentee is progressing through the SOC-to-DFIR pathway, and the transition is ongoing.
evidence.followup: The pathway provides my mentee and me with an agreed set of development objectives to work through.

evidence.title: Threat intelligence webinar series
evidence.situation: There was an opportunity to share current threat intelligence more widely with clients and the security community.
evidence.task: To devise and deliver a regular threat intelligence webinar, open to all, which I have run across my last two roles.
evidence.action: I curate each session from current threat reporting and present it live, explaining the practical implications for both practitioners and non-specialists. The webinar is promoted on LinkedIn by my organisation and me.
evidence.result: Feedback has been positive, and attendance records show a high proportion of returning attendees. Without advertising, the webinar has grown from zero to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries at the most recent session.
evidence.followup: In response to attendee feedback, I moved from broad monthly sessions to quarterly sector-focused webinars, including an in-depth session on transport and logistics.

evidence.title: Guest on the Richmond Advisory Group "Cyber Sidekicks" podcast
evidence.situation: During Cyber Awareness Month in October 2025, I was invited, as Technical Director at CyXcel, to appear as a guest on the Richmond Advisory Group's "Cyber Sidekicks" podcast.
evidence.task: To share practical insight from DFIR with a business audience.
evidence.action: I discussed current developments in artificial intelligence and DFIR, and how organisations can strengthen their cyber resilience.
evidence.result: The episode was published and remains publicly available.

evidence.title: ISO/IEC 27001, NCSC CIR (Standard) and Cyber Essentials accreditation in first year as DFIR lead
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead of a newly established team handling highly sensitive client evidence, I recognised the importance of industry-recognised accreditations to demonstrate assurance to clients and insurers.
evidence.task: To achieve ISO/IEC 27001, the NCSC CIR scheme at Standard level and Cyber Essentials within my first year as DFIR lead, under the sponsorship of the chief executive.
evidence.action: As the team was being established from scratch and the accreditations were year-one objectives, I designed our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset rather than retrofitting controls. I scheduled audits and assessments well in advance, used a dashboard to track and validate outstanding actions ahead of each assessment, held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to audit preparation, and regularly verified that our practices remained aligned.
evidence.result: The team passed all three audits and assessments at the first attempt, within my first year as DFIR lead.
evidence.followup: I maintain an audit trail of everything each accreditation requires us to evidence and ensure it is updated monthly. Under the NCSC CIR scheme, I report monthly on the number and types of incidents investigated. For ISO/IEC 27001, I assess any new technology or infrastructure against the standard's requirements before it is introduced. The objective is not only to meet each requirement but to be able to evidence it at audit.

evidence.title: Threat intelligence service design and launch
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead, I recognised threat intelligence as essential both to support investigations and to help prevent incidents. Without an intelligence capability, the team was limited in its ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour and advise clients beyond the immediate incident. There was also a commercial opportunity, as clients were increasingly seeking a service combining reactive and proactive support. I had built a comparable service in my previous role, where it generated 15% of total incident response revenue across reactive work and retainers.
evidence.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a threat intelligence offering with two objectives: strengthening our incident response capability with timely intelligence, and establishing a standalone service with a clear market differentiator.
evidence.action: I structured the workstream around the intelligence lifecycle, from direction and collection through analysis and dissemination, and evaluated several commercial intelligence products to complement the team's own dark web persona footprint, capability and open-source tooling. Beyond monitoring each client's own exposure, the service mapped critical suppliers through stakeholder interviews and monitored them for indicators of risk, for example a supplier with 50 infostealer infections in the past month, or a supplier holding client data that had suffered a ransomware attack, consistent with NCSC supply chain security guidance. I trained new starters to support threat intelligence from day one using defined methodologies, templates and tooling, and launched the service in partnership with the marketing team.
evidence.result: Intelligence rapidly became integral to our incident response process: from the outset, the team gathered current TTPs, IOCs and campaign intelligence to support engagements, accelerating the detection of malicious activity. The service was well received by clients, and supply chain coverage was a key factor in its success, particularly as the launch coincided with several high-profile ransomware incidents enabled by supply chain compromise.

evidence.title: OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp and MetaDefender certification
evidence.situation: Protecting CNI and OT is a fast-moving, specialised field in which threats can rapidly escalate into critical incidents. Formal training is important both for organisational capability and for my own professional development in this area.
evidence.task: To complete the OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp and its certification, deepening my expertise in CNI protection, OT and ICS security and threat prevention, and contributing CPD towards my certifications and professional memberships.
evidence.action: I completed the two-day, in-person OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp.
evidence.result: I achieved the OPSWAT certification for the MetaDefender platform and recorded the CPD in my SANS account towards GCFA renewal.

evidence.title: fx: open-source forensic triage and threat-hunting tool
evidence.situation: DFIR practitioners rely on a range of commercial tools, alongside established open-source resources such as Eric Zimmerman's tools, Autopsy, Chainsaw and Hayabusa. I identified the need for a graphical triage tool that would complement both, with the added value of automated threat hunting against the TTPs of common financially motivated threat actors.
evidence.task: I researched the tools in common use and the capabilities that would add most value. A frequently overlooked area was automated hunting for the known TTPs and IOCs of the most prolific ransomware groups. Other essential requirements included a visual timeline for identifying spikes in activity, the ability to pivot around events, and the ability to tag and export artefacts.
evidence.action: I built the tool from first principles, using AI-assisted development. It parses a range of Windows host artefacts, including the MFT, EVTX logs, Prefetch, Amcache/Shimcache and browser history, hashing every evidence item and maintaining an ingest log to preserve evidential integrity in line with ISO/IEC 27037. Threat hunting runs in the background, presenting findings rated critical, high or medium for analyst review. Analysts can tag items, pivot around findings, view an activity graph to identify anomalous spikes, search the data and ingest IOC lists for bulk queries. Findings are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and can be exported in multiple formats, including CSV, STIX and HTML.
evidence.result: fx v0.1.4 is publicly released on GitHub and has been used on live investigations by me and other practitioners. Named industry practitioners testing the tool have given positive feedback on its ability to identify malicious activity and have suggested future enhancements.
evidence.followup: fx remains under active development, and I continue to incorporate user feedback into its roadmap.

evidence.title: Open-source toolkit for incident response, readiness, intelligence and OT
evidence.situation: DFIR and intelligence work frequently takes place in isolated or air-gapped environments, or on client sites without approved tooling. Commercial and open-source tools are often fragmented, sit behind paywalls or operate as cloud services to which sensitive data cannot be uploaded.
evidence.task: To create a suite of free, open-source tools covering the incident response lifecycle and the readiness and assessment activity that supports it.
evidence.action: I designed and built a suite of fully client-side tools in HTML, using AI-assisted development. The suite spans the incident lifecycle, from TRACE for case management to email header and PowerShell analysis, file hashing and text comparison, alongside MITRE ATT&CK mapping, threat actor references, and assessment tools aligned to the NCSC CAF, cyber and phishing programme maturity models, and OT field and reference guides. Each tool is mapped to recognised frameworks, and the collection is openly published on GitHub.
evidence.result: The result is a free, open-source toolkit of more than 40 tools that operate anywhere without uploading data, supporting responders across the whole incident lifecycle.

evidence.title: Technical commentary on the DDoS attack on X (Times Radio / Daily Mail coverage)
evidence.situation: On 10 March 2025, X (formerly Twitter) suffered a significant DDoS attack that caused outages for users worldwide over several hours.
evidence.task: To support my organisation's media response: a colleague was interviewed by Times Radio and the Daily Mail, and I provided the detailed technical analysis.
evidence.action: I explained how the attack unfolded in multiple waves throughout the day, which group had claimed responsibility, and the measures organisations can take to protect themselves against DDoS attacks.
evidence.result: My organisation published my analysis on LinkedIn alongside the Times Radio interview and the Daily Mail article.

evidence.title: LinkedIn recommendation for a former colleague
evidence.situation: A former colleague asked me for a LinkedIn recommendation to support their search for a new role.
evidence.task: To provide a professional recommendation in support of their job search.
evidence.action: I wrote and published a LinkedIn recommendation reflecting their skills and contribution.
evidence.result: The recommendation is published on their LinkedIn profile in support of their search.

evidence.title: Article contribution for the Daily Mail on SMS security risks
evidence.situation: My organisation was asked to contribute to a Daily Mail article on the security risks posed by SMS text messaging.
evidence.task: At the request of our marketing team, I wrote a 750-word article for a general readership outlining the principal risks of SMS messaging, to a tight publication deadline.
evidence.action: I produced an article to the brief, covering social engineering, spoofing and misplaced trust, the weaknesses of SMS-based authentication, and malware and device risks, together with practical mitigations aligned to NCSC guidance for the public.
evidence.result: An excerpt from my article was published in the Daily Mail in February 2025.

evidence.title: Community sharing of phishing domains following the CrowdStrike outage
evidence.situation: Following the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024, caused by a faulty software update, new CrowdStrike-themed domains were being registered daily, many of them likely to be used for phishing and malware distribution.
evidence.task: To collate newly registered suspicious domains and share them with the security community.
evidence.action: From 20 July 2024, I collated newly registered CrowdStrike-themed domains in a shared Google Sheet, highlighting each day's additions, and published daily updates on X and LinkedIn, tagging other researchers tracking the same activity.
evidence.result: Individual updates reached between 160 and 180 views each, giving defenders a free, current list of suspicious domains to block or monitor.

evidence.title: Conference attendance (Black Hat, BSides, Infosecurity Europe)
evidence.situation: DFIR and threat intelligence evolve rapidly, as do attacker TTPs and investigative tooling, particularly with the growth of AI, and much of that knowledge emerges at conferences and within the communities around them.
evidence.task: To maintain current DFIR and CTI knowledge and engage with peers through a deliberate mix of commercial and community conferences: Black Hat for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability, Infosecurity Europe for the broader market and governance landscape, and BSides for practitioner-led content and professional networking.
evidence.action: I attend these events regularly: I have attended Black Hat for the past three years, as well as Infosecurity Europe, and will attend Black Hat and BSides London in December 2026. I have also presented at events, including a talk to the Bedford branch of BCS while in law enforcement, and lectures to police colleagues on the dark web, section 49 of RIPA 2000, cyber crime and digital currencies.
evidence.result: This activity contributes to my 20 to 40 hours of formal CPD each year, recorded in my SANS account towards GCFA renewal.

evidence.title: Professional membership: CIISec
evidence.situation: I am an Affiliate member of CIISec through my employer.
evidence.task: To work in accordance with the CIISec Code of Conduct.
evidence.action: I apply its principles in my casework, for example by obtaining written authorisation before accessing personal data.
evidence.result: EV-027 provides an example of the Code informing a decision in practice.

evidence.title: High-volume, insurance-led incident response
evidence.scale: 500+ incident response engagements over the past five years in consultancy roles
evidence.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles, I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many of them insurance-led.
evidence.task: To lead investigations into ransomware, nation-state activity, BEC, network intrusion and other incident types, while managing clients, budgets and investigation teams.
evidence.action: I led investigations across these incident types in line with the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, managing the client relationship, engagement budget and investigation team on each.
evidence.result: During this period, my firm held positions on six to ten insurer panels for large global organisations across EMEA, principally in the UK, with significant work in South Africa.

evidence.title: Examining locked devices under legal authority (policing)
evidence.situation: In my policing role, I routinely examined devices that were locked or for which passcodes were unavailable.
evidence.task: To recover evidence from these devices lawfully, within the legal framework and under the required authority.
evidence.action: I used specialist tools including GrayKey and Cellebrite, completed training in Android debugging, and used password-recovery tools in Kali Linux, alongside the examination of other seized devices to help identify passcodes. All work followed the ACPO principles for digital evidence.
evidence.result: All examinations were conducted within the legal framework and under the required authority.

evidence.title: DFIR budget ownership as technical director
evidence.situation: As technical director, I was responsible for the DFIR function's expenditure, including the establishment of a UK forensic laboratory.
evidence.task: To set budgets across tooling, personnel and laboratory expenditure.
evidence.action: I produced a detailed budget assessment covering tooling, personnel and laboratory expenditure, aligned to forecast revenue, and repurposed existing equipment where possible to reduce laboratory costs.
evidence.result: The budget was approved following review. Laboratory expenditure came in slightly under budget, and the laboratory was delivered on time with fully operational, secure infrastructure that met all requirements.

evidence.title: Lunch-and-learn sessions (memory forensics, incident response, threat intelligence, evidence integrity)
evidence.scale: Four to five sessions, each with 5 to 15 attendees
evidence.situation: I identified a need to develop the team's DFIR capability alongside live casework and to address recurring issues, such as incomplete chain of custody records.
evidence.task: To share specialist knowledge across the team and ensure that colleagues understood their evidential and legal obligations.
evidence.action: I designed and delivered four to five lunch-and-learn sessions: memory forensics using Volatility; incident response; threat intelligence, covering OSINT good practice and operational security, particularly on the dark web; and evidence integrity. The evidence integrity session, based on the ACPO principles and ISO/IEC 27037, covered how chain of custody is documented and recorded in our systems, the information required on evidence bags, photographing evidence items (particularly damaged items) and, where possible, recording the disassembly of devices, so that the handling of each item can be reproduced and withstands legal scrutiny.
evidence.result: Each session was attended by between 5 and 15 team members, with senior management attending on occasion, and feedback was positive.
evidence.followup: I circulated the slides after each session and invited follow-up questions.

evidence.title: Impartial, evidence-based reporting and expert evidence
evidence.situation: As an expert witness and the author of incident reports, my findings may be relied upon by courts, regulators, insurers and boards. In DFIR it is common to be unable to establish root cause conclusively, for example due to limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensic activity, and clients can perceive this as a failure.
evidence.task: To ensure every finding is impartial and evidence-based, irrespective of the outcome the client may prefer.
evidence.action: As an expert witness, I recognised that my role was impartial and that my overriding duty was to the court, with my evidence based solely on fact or, where gaps existed, on clearly identified expert opinion. I include findings in a report only where they are corroborated by evidence. Where root cause cannot be established, I explain the reasons fully rather than speculating. If I am asked to overstate a finding, I decline and explain that, as the report's author, I could be held liable for any statement I know to be untrue.
evidence.result: In one engagement, this meant reporting data exfiltration the client had hoped to rule out; the client accepted the report as written and notified the ICO (see EV-026).

evidence.title: Calm, transparent communication with a client under pressure during ransomware recovery
evidence.situation: A manufacturer's encrypted systems had halted most of its operational capability, with losses exceeding £1 million per day, and its leadership was under intense pressure.
evidence.task: To lead the response and provide the client's leadership with the information it needed to make decisions under pressure.
evidence.action: I provided calm, clear briefings on the recovery process, likely timescales and how quickly the systems supporting manufacturing could be restored. Rapid restoration required the client to accept residual risk, which I explained transparently: the systems appeared clean but were not yet validated as free of malware or persistent access, and good practice would be to keep them isolated until that was confirmed.
evidence.result: The team restored critical manufacturing processes within 48 hours. The client understood and accepted the residual risk, and subsequent checks confirmed the hosts were clean, allowing production to resume.

evidence.title: Fair and consistent recruitment: graduate scheme and structured interviews
evidence.situation: In a previous role, we needed to grow the team and bring new talent into the profession fairly.
evidence.task: To recruit on the value candidates could bring, never on any characteristic protected under the Equality Act 2010.
evidence.action: We operated a graduate scheme that brought final-year university students into the profession through a structured training pathway and a ten-week placement leading to permanent roles. In interviews, we used a consistent question set for every candidate, so that we assessed competencies fairly. I also took part in my employer's community volunteering programme, supporting causes such as homelessness charities.
evidence.result: The graduate scheme brought several junior team members into the profession.

evidence.title: Reporting data exfiltration the client had ruled out
evidence.situation: A client's internal investigation had found no evidence of data exfiltration. My investigation identified evidence in the logs that personal and sensitive data had been exfiltrated, engaging notification obligations to the ICO and to affected individuals under Articles 33 and 34 of the UK GDPR, with potential regulatory penalties.
evidence.task: To report the findings accurately, as investigation lead and report author.
evidence.action: I was asked to understate the finding in the report and declined: the evidence in the logs was unambiguous, the report had to reflect it, and the client, as data controller, had a statutory obligation to notify.
evidence.result: The client accepted the report as written and notified the ICO. My team supported the notification and used e-discovery tools to assess the exfiltrated data and identify the affected data subjects.

evidence.title: Written authorisation before accessing a cloud mailbox
evidence.situation: In the civil litigation matter, the client provided a username, password and verbal permission to access a former employee's Gmail account.
evidence.task: To access the evidence only under proper authority.
evidence.action: I judged that verbal permission was insufficient, as accessing an account without the owner's authority risks an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990. Before proceeding, I obtained written authorisation from both the client and the account owner and confirmed the legal basis for access.
evidence.result: I accessed the mailbox only once written authorisation and the legal basis were confirmed, so the evidence could be relied upon in court.

evidence.title: Developing a multinational DFIR team (previous role)
evidence.situation: In my previous role, the DFIR practice comprised 15 to 20 staff in the UK, 20 to 30 in the United States and five to ten in India, with line managers at each grade conducting monthly and annual performance reviews.
evidence.task: To ensure that the people I led were on track and had a clear route to progression, with training that met both their individual needs and those of the business, within the training budget.
evidence.action: I held check-ins at least quarterly to confirm that individuals were on track and that their training needs were being met, and to understand informally whether they were content and what further support they needed. We operated a structured training pathway supported by a learning platform. I identified specialist paid training, such as SANS and Firebrand courses, where it served both an individual's route to the next grade and a capability the business needed, balancing this against the training budget.
evidence.result: On several occasions, staff were promoted to the next grade with additional responsibilities.

evidence.title: Forensic methodology documents (Windows, Linux, Mac, cloud)
evidence.situation: Analysts need a structured, repeatable approach to investigations across operating systems and cloud platforms. Repeatability means every investigation is carried out consistently, whoever conducts it, so that key artefacts are not missed under pressure. Findings can then be reproduced by an independent examiner, in line with the ACPO principles, and withstand legal and regulatory scrutiny. It also helps new analysts become effective quickly.
evidence.task: To develop and maintain a forensic methodology aligned to recognised frameworks.
evidence.action: I wrote our methodology documents, covering Windows, Linux and Mac forensics, as well as AWS, GCP and Azure, aligned to the NIST SP 800-61r3 and SANS incident response frameworks and the ACPO principles. Before each document was adopted, other members of the team reviewed and validated it. I continually update the documents to reflect changes in attacker TTPs, including the growing use of AI in attacks, so that analysts can identify AI-enabled activity. Lessons learned from each engagement also feed back into them..
evidence.result: Analysts work to a consistent, peer-validated and repeatable approach that keeps pace with evolving attacker methods and produces defensible findings.

evidence.title: Tracking legal and regulatory change
evidence.situation: Much of my current work is with clients in regulated sectors, organisations holding sensitive or personal data, and those operating in CNI sectors, all of which face evolving legal and regulatory requirements.
evidence.task: To maintain current legal and regulatory knowledge in a structured, sustainable way.
evidence.action: I follow a structured process built on authoritative sources: NCSC alerts and guidance, ICO updates, professional events and communities, and forthcoming legislation such as the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which will update the NIS Regulations 2018. My work also takes account of the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
evidence.result: This informs the design of the UK forensic lab, so that clients can comply with new requirements from the outset.

evidence.title: Resolving executive and IT conflict over ransomware recovery timescales
evidence.situation: A medium-sized organisation suffered a ransomware attack on a Friday evening. Its executives expected the business to be fully operational by Monday morning, while the IT team advised that this could not be achieved in the time available.
evidence.task: To lead the response and agree a recovery plan to which both the executives and the IT team could commit.
evidence.action: I explained that full recovery from ransomware within that timeframe was rarely achievable for an organisation of this size, and took both groups through the recovery process using my firm's ransomware timeline, which sets out the typical stages from attack to recovery for organisations with no prior experience of an incident. Together we agreed to prioritise business-critical systems: those that were customer-facing or essential to operations. I explained the residual risk that restored systems could be brought online in a new environment but could not yet be confirmed as fully clean. The client accepted that risk, and the IT team built a new environment for the restored systems.
evidence.result: Business-critical systems were restored first, allowing core operations to continue, and the remainder of remediation followed agreed, tested processes.

evidence.title: Two-way peer review of client reports
evidence.situation: Every report the team delivers may be relied upon by clients, insurers and regulators, and contains confidential client information.
evidence.task: To ensure that every report meets the highest standards of quality and accuracy before it reaches the client.
evidence.action: All reports are peer reviewed before delivery: I review team members' reports, and I ask a colleague to review mine objectively and recommend improvements. In one review, I identified that a team member had reused a previous report as a template and that it still contained another client's information. I discussed with them why the clean master template had not been used (the case closely resembled a recent engagement) and reinforced our policy, which defines a clean template for each stage of the incident lifecycle and requires every incident to begin from new templates.
evidence.result: The other client's information was removed before the report was issued, preventing a breach of confidentiality and of our UK GDPR obligations. The team member accepted the guidance, and the matter was resolved informally.

evidence.title: Adapting scope when an undisclosed development environment emerged
evidence.situation: Insurance-led engagements often begin with no knowledge of the client's environment, and initial scoping can miss key information where the right stakeholders are unavailable or the right questions have not been asked. In one compromise, my team's analysis identified lateral movement from a development environment that had not been disclosed during scoping and was outside the agreed scope.
evidence.task: To follow the incident response lifecycle, aligned to NIST SP 800-61, while adapting the plan as new information emerged.
evidence.action: After scoping, I hold an additional technical call with the client's IT team to identify gaps early. When the development environment came to light, I engaged the client's technical team, who confirmed it was connected to production. I explained transparently to the client what had originally been planned, what was now required and why, and the revised cost, and obtained approval from the client or its insurer before the additional work began.
evidence.result: With approval in place, the team assessed the development environment and established that the threat actor had gained initial access through it, identifying the root cause.

evidence.title: Addressing an incomplete chain of custody record
evidence.situation: A team member submitted a chain of custody record that was incomplete, which meant the missing details had to be validated after the event and made the evidence harder to verify.
evidence.task: The record was completed and the evidence’s integrity preserved. The team was briefed on exactly what to record, so that the handling of every evidence item can be reproduced and withstand legal scrutiny.
evidence.action: I worked with the team member to validate and complete the missing information, and discussed with them why each element of the record matters. I then used the occasion as a learning point for the wider team, delivering a lunch-and-learn session on evidence integrity based on the ACPO principles and ISO/IEC 27037
evidence.result: The team was briefed on precisely what to record so that the handling of every evidence item can be reproduced and withstands legal scrutiny.

evidence.title: Planning and reviewing training against individual and business needs
evidence.situation: In my previous role, the team's training needed to be planned in advance and assessed against both operational requirements and the progression needs of individuals.
evidence.task: To plan training that met the needs of both the business and the individual, within the training budget, and to review whether it had delivered value.
evidence.action: The senior leadership team held a monthly training call, which I contributed to, setting out projected training requirements against operational needs and budget. In one-to-ones and appraisals, I then reviewed each person's learning with them: what they had completed, how useful they had found it and whether it had since added value to their work.
evidence.result: These reviews informed future training requirements for the wider team, so that investment was directed at training that had proved its worth. My own development is reviewed in the same way by my line manager.

A1.situation: A multinational telecommunications provider suffered a double-extortion ransomware attack that encrypted servers across several countries, exfiltrated data and disrupted telephony services for some customers. The client's cyber insurer referred the engagement to my firm, so we had no prior relationship with the organisation or knowledge of its environment. Stakeholders included the executive, IT and legal teams, the data protection officer, the insurer and external counsel.
A1.task: As engagement lead, I was accountable for the DFIR response end to end, including the investigation team, client reporting and cost reporting to the insurer. The priorities were to restore telephony, then critical and wider business services, while supporting the client's regulatory obligations across several jurisdictions.
A1.action: In the first hours, the stakeholders on the call could not confirm whether the network was segmented. I recommended immediate network isolation to contain the attack. This carried significant business disruption, but further encryption would have delayed recovery by weeks and widened the impact on customers, so I judged it the lower risk. I ran the response in line with the NIST SP 800-61r3 lifecycle, leading a team of five to ten. I initially split the team between containment and gathering the IOCs and evidence of persistence needed for recovery, such as C2 channels and backdoors, mapping attacker activity to MITRE ATT&CK. We restored only from backups that triage had verified as clean. Once critical services were running, I moved the team on to root cause analysis, validating the attacker's data theft claims and eradicating persistence, and recovered hosts through an isolated, EDR-monitored network zone before returning them to production.
A1.result: The client's infrastructure team later confirmed that the network was not fully segmented; without isolation, further systems would have been encrypted and more services affected. The team restored customer-facing services within 48 hours and most critical services within a week, with full restoration confirmed after approximately three months.
A1.followup: I led a post-incident review, assigning an owner to each improvement action. Despite having no previous relationship with my firm, the client went on to retain us for a substantial readiness programme and a multi-year managed service.

A2.situation: A manufacturing company brought civil proceedings against a former employee who had left to set up a competing business in Malaysia, using lower-cost production tooling and labour. The company alleged that he had taken a significant volume of its intellectual property, and any findings would need to withstand scrutiny in court.
A2.task: I was instructed to examine more than 15 devices and accounts, including laptops, mobile phones, external media, cloud storage and email, and was responsible for establishing whether the evidence supported the allegations. A court order defined the scope of my authority. I drew on my policing background, where I routinely examined devices, including locked devices, under the appropriate legal authority.
A2.action: I carried out the examination in accordance with the ACPO principles and ISO/IEC 27037, so that the original evidence remained unaltered and an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. Each device was received powered off; I photographed it, acquired a physical image, verified the acquisition by hash and maintained chain of custody throughout, keeping contemporaneous notes and photographic records. I conducted the analysis on a dedicated, forensically clean workstation using commercial tools in which I am trained and experienced. While most devices showed no relevant activity, an iCloud backup on a Mac contained a messaging conversation that provided compelling evidence of the allegation, together with web searches relating to data destruction and clearing search history. That conversation led me to a second messaging application, which the former employee had described as "not on their radar", containing evidence of extensive data theft.
A2.result: My examination found clear evidence that the company's intellectual property had been taken without authority, and I set out my findings in an affidavit.
A2.followup: I subsequently gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the company succeeded in its claim.

A3.situation: My firm took over a range of managed services for a client, including DFIR, from a previous third-party provider. During the handover I identified that the client's incident response plan (IRP) was out of date and that it had no scenario-specific runbooks, leaving a material gap in its preparedness.
A3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a new IRP and runbooks for the client's most likely and highest-impact scenarios. I selected six scenarios based on threat intelligence relevant to the client's sector and geography and agreed them with the client, which retained formal approval of the plan.
A3.action: I aligned the IRP to NIST SP 800-61r3 and ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications, communication channels and escalation routes. Each runbook set out step-by-step procedures for detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Rather than relying on untested guidance, I validated every command and KQL query in the client's live environment to confirm that it worked and was appropriate.
A3.result: The client formally approved the IRP and all six runbooks, which are now the standard for its SOC and incident response teams.
A3.followup: I introduced an annual review cycle, with additional reviews following any significant vendor or network change. The runbooks have since been used in live incidents, and the lessons-learned review I facilitate after each one, with senior stakeholders and key responders, feeds into the next version.

B1.situation: A global news organisation had experienced an incident in which malware on a personal (BYOD) device reached its corporate network. Although the attack was unsuccessful and the vulnerabilities had been remediated, unclear decision-making had slowed the response, and the client wished to test its decision-making. Executives from London, Germany and Hong Kong attended in person, alongside key IT stakeholders.
B1.task: I was responsible for designing and facilitating a tabletop exercise to assess the organisation's readiness for a significant malware incident, test its incident response plan and identify gaps in decision-making and coordination. The client retained ownership of the resulting decisions and actions.
B1.action: I began by listening: scoping sessions with the IT team established their bespoke and commercial tooling, the circumstances of the near miss and the objectives for the exercise. I developed the real incident into a significant malware attack involving data exfiltration and extortion, informed by current threat actor tactics. Timed injects tested strategic and technical decision-making, business impact and prioritisation, regulatory notification, ransom and sanctions considerations, and media handling. I facilitated the discussion between executives and IT stakeholders while my team recorded decisions in real time. I challenged a key assumption by asking how decisions would be made if the named decision-makers were unavailable: the playbook assigned critical business decisions to individuals with no deputies, which prompted a discussion of delegated authority for time-critical decisions.
B1.result: Client feedback was positive, and the exercise identified several gaps, which I documented with recommendations in a post-exercise report.
B1.followup: At a follow-up meeting with the IT team, I agreed the recommendations and assigned owners and deadlines. Through regular progress meetings as part of our ongoing relationship, I have confirmed that the client now conducts practical testing of procedures that previously existed only in documentation, including backup retrieval and restoration.

B2.situation: During a multinational ransomware response, several key business systems could not be recovered from backups and would otherwise have required rebuilding at significant cost and time. The client's board needed to decide whether to engage with the threat actor, a decision carrying legal, sanctions, financial and reputational risk.
B2.task: I led the threat actor engagement workstream and was responsible for advising the board. The decision rested with the board, advised by its legal counsel and cyber insurer.
B2.action: I initially used engagement to establish whether data had in fact been exfiltrated and to understand the threat actor's demands, so that the board's decision was based on evidence rather than the attacker's claims. I then set out the risks in clear, non-technical terms: a decryptor might not be provided; any decryptor was unlikely to be fully reliable, particularly on large datasets; re-infection and further extortion remained possible; and assurances that stolen data would be deleted could not be verified. This advice drew on my firm's experience of the threat actor and on input from trusted cryptocurrency partners. I explained the sanctions due diligence required, including screening against the UK OFSI and US OFAC sanctions lists, and my team completed these checks on the client's behalf. In parallel, I advised on regulatory notifications across several jurisdictions, including to the ICO.
B2.result: The sanctions checks confirmed that engagement could proceed lawfully. My workstream secured a substantial reduction in the original demand, and the decryption tool significantly accelerated the recovery of systems that could not otherwise have been restored quickly.
B2.followup: With a clear understanding of the risks, the board scrutinised its options more rigorously. In my experience, the decision to engage is usually driven by necessity, such as the absence of viable backups or the sensitivity of the data at risk, so I ensure that boards understand the risks well before that point.

B3.situation: Across more than 500 incident response engagements, I have supported IT teams, chief information security officers and staff operating under intense pressure. In one ransomware attack on a manufacturer, encrypted systems had halted most operational capability, with losses exceeding £1 million per day, and leadership needed to decide which parts of the business to restore first.
B3.task: I led the response and was responsible for supporting the client's people through it; decisions on restoration priorities and risk acceptance rested with the client. In a previous role I also contributed to recruitment, where I was responsible for assessing candidates fairly.
B3.action: I provided calm, clear briefings on the recovery process, likely timescales and how quickly the systems supporting manufacturing could be restored, enabling leadership to make informed decisions on restoration priorities. Rapid restoration required the client to accept residual risk, which I explained transparently: the systems appeared clean but were not yet validated as free of malware or persistent access, and good practice would be to keep them isolated until that was confirmed. In recruitment, I assess candidates solely on the value they can bring, never on any characteristic protected under the Equality Act 2010. We used structured interviews with a consistent question set, so that we assessed competencies fairly, and a graduate scheme that brought final-year university students into the profession through a structured training pathway and a ten-week placement leading to permanent roles. I also took part in my employer's community volunteering programme, supporting causes such as homelessness charities.
B3.result: The team restored critical manufacturing processes within 48 hours. The client understood and accepted the residual risk, and subsequent checks confirmed the hosts were clean, allowing production to resume. The graduate scheme brought several junior team members into the profession.
B3.followup: I apply the same approach on every engagement: keeping clients calm and informed, and being transparent about the risks of each recovery option so that they can make informed decisions.

B4.situation: Threat intelligence and cyber risk must be communicated to very different audiences, from security practitioners to members of the public with no technical background.
B4.task: I am responsible for curating and presenting a regular threat intelligence webinar, open to all, which I have run across my last two roles. Separately, my organisation's marketing team commissioned me to write a 750-word article for the Daily Mail on the risks of SMS messaging, to a tight publication deadline.
B4.action: For the webinar, I select current threats and explain their practical implications for an audience of both practitioners and non-specialists. For the article, I wrote for a general readership, explaining social engineering, spoofing and misplaced trust in text messages, the weaknesses of SMS-based authentication, and malware and device risks, together with practical protective measures. When a colleague was interviewed by Times Radio about the DDoS attack on X (formerly Twitter) in March 2025, I provided the accompanying technical analysis of how the attack unfolded and how organisations can protect themselves. I apply the same principle to incident reporting: I typically produce an executive report focused on cost, downtime, operational impact and reputation, with a concise account of what happened and why, alongside a detailed technical report containing full findings and recommendations for IT teams.
B4.result: Feedback on the webinar has been positive, and attendance records show a high proportion of returning attendees. Without advertising, it has grown from zero to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries at the most recent session. The Daily Mail published an excerpt of my article in February 2025.
B4.followup: In response to attendee feedback, I moved from broad monthly sessions to quarterly sector-focused webinars, including an in-depth session on transport and logistics.

C1.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles, I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many referred by cyber insurers, covering ransomware, nation-state activity, BEC and network intrusion. My firm held positions on six to ten insurer panels across EMEA, principally in the UK and South Africa. Insurers fund these engagements and require accurate cost forecasting and regular reporting.
C1.task: On the engagements I led, I was responsible for the investigation team, the client relationship and cost reporting, with the insurer approving expenditure. As technical director, I was also responsible for setting the DFIR budget across tooling, personnel and laboratory expenditure.
C1.action: I produced a detailed budget assessment covering tooling, personnel and laboratory expenditure, aligned to forecast revenue. On the largest engagement, a three-month multinational ransomware response, I provided the insurer with a projected run rate at the outset and submitted weekly cost reports for approval. I led up to ten people at any one time, initially dividing the team broadly equally between containment and evidence collection to support recovery, before redeploying effort to root cause analysis and validated recovery. The first week required sustained long hours, so I held regular individual check-ins to understand how each person was coping and what support they needed. As the tempo reduced, I rotated staff on and off the engagement, using capacity around training and leave, to give people a break from the investigation.
C1.result: Costs tracked closely to the projected run rate and were approved by the insurer each week. Customer-facing services were restored within 48 hours and most critical services within a week.
C1.followup: The client was highly satisfied with the outcome and subsequently invested a six-figure sum in proactive services as part of an ongoing relationship.

C2.situation: In my previous role, the DFIR practice comprised 15 to 20 staff in the UK, 20 to 30 in the United States and five to ten in India. Line managers at each grade supported the staff in the grade below and conducted monthly and annual performance reviews.
C2.task: I was responsible for developing the people I led, ensuring that their training met both their own progression needs and the operational needs of the business, within the training budget.
C2.action: I held check-ins at least quarterly to confirm that individuals were on track, that their training needs were being met and that they had the skills their work required, and to understand informally whether they were content and what further support they needed. We operated a structured training pathway supported by a learning platform. I identified specialist paid training, such as SANS and Firebrand courses, where it served both an individual's route to the next grade and a capability the business needed, balancing this against the training budget. I also delivered lunch-and-learn sessions on memory forensics using Volatility, incident response, threat intelligence, and evidence integrity under the ACPO principles.
C2.result: On several occasions, staff were promoted to the next grade with additional responsibilities, confirmed through the formal performance review process.
C2.followup: I apply the same approach in my current role. I train new starters to support threat intelligence from day one using defined methodologies, templates and tooling, and I have developed six career frameworks aligned to SFIA 9 to provide clear routes for progression. I also mentor a junior colleague transitioning from the SOC into DFIR.

C3.situation: A global news organisation, an existing client, commissioned an in-person executive tabletop exercise following a near miss, with participants from London, Germany and Hong Kong. As many attendees were non-technical, the exercise needed to feel familiar and realistic, run to time and produce actionable outcomes.
C3.task: I was responsible for planning and delivering the exercise end to end within three to four weeks. I designed the exercise personally and directed two researchers supporting its preparation.
C3.action: I began with a call to agree the client's objectives, attendees and desired outcomes. I built the scenario around the client's own in-house and proprietary systems, so that non-technical attendees would recognise the applications, their functions and the data they held, and produced a delegate briefing pack describing the systems and each attendee's role. My researchers supported the scenario with research into current threat actor tactics. I ran two internal rehearsals, which identified injects that were sound in theory but did not work in practice, and refined them before delivery. On the day, I kept the timed injects to schedule while my team recorded decisions in real time. Afterwards, I produced a comprehensive report setting out the lessons learned and a full record of the discussion.
C3.result: The exercise ran to schedule and identified several gaps. Around two weeks later, I met the IT team that had commissioned it; having gathered feedback from attendees, they agreed several practical improvements for immediate implementation and a roadmap for further changes.
C3.followup: I monitor progress against the roadmap through monthly calls with the client.

C4.situation: As DFIR lead, I am responsible for highly sensitive client evidence, including legally privileged material. The team was being established from scratch, and the chief executive set ISO/IEC 27001, the NCSC CIR scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials as objectives for my first year.
C4.task: I was responsible for achieving all three accreditations, under the chief executive's sponsorship, and for ensuring that the team operated to them day to day.
C4.action: Because the accreditations were year-one objectives, I designed our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset rather than retrofitting controls. I scheduled audits and assessments well in advance, used a dashboard to track and validate outstanding actions ahead of each assessment, and held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to audit preparation. Between assessments, I regularly verified that our practices remained aligned. I apply the same discipline to casework: evidence is processed on dedicated, forensically clean workstations, every acquisition is hash-verified, chain of custody is maintained in line with ISO/IEC 27037, and all actions are recorded so that an independent examiner could reproduce the findings. Client updates on incident response engagements are provided under legal privilege.
C4.result: The team passed all three audits and assessments at the first attempt, within my first year as DFIR lead.
C4.followup: I maintain an audit trail of everything each accreditation requires us to evidence and ensure it is updated monthly. Under the NCSC CIR scheme, I report monthly on the number and types of incidents investigated. For ISO/IEC 27001, I assess any new technology or infrastructure against the standard's requirements before it is introduced. The objective is not only to meet each requirement but to be able to evidence it at audit.

D1.situation: I served 13 years in policing, where honesty and integrity underpin every investigation, and I apply the same standard to incident response. In one engagement, the client's internal investigation had found no evidence of data exfiltration. My investigation identified evidence in the logs that personal and sensitive data had been exfiltrated, engaging notification obligations to the ICO and affected individuals under Articles 33 and 34 of the UK GDPR, with potential regulatory penalties.
D1.task: As investigation lead and report author, I was responsible for reporting the findings accurately. The decision to notify rested with the client as data controller, which was legally obliged to do so where a reportable breach had occurred.
D1.action: I was asked to understate the finding in the report and declined. My reports are based on facts and evidence, with expert opinion confined to genuine gaps and clearly identified as such. In this case the evidence was unambiguous: the logs showed a defined volume of data leaving the network. I explained that the report had to reflect the evidence and that the client had a statutory obligation to notify. Whenever I am asked to alter a finding, I also make clear that, as the report's author, I could be held liable for any statement I know to be untrue.
D1.result: The client accepted the report as written and notified the ICO. My team supported the notification and used e-discovery tools to assess the exfiltrated data and identify the affected data subjects.
D1.followup: I apply the same principle where root cause cannot be established, for example due to limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensic activity. Clients can perceive this as a failure, so I explain the reasons fully rather than offering speculation.

D2.situation: Forensic investigation frequently requires access to personal data, such as email accounts and cloud storage, where acting without proper authority could breach the law and cause harm to those involved. In a civil litigation matter, the client provided a username, password and verbal permission to examine a former employee's Gmail account.
D2.task: I am bound by the codes and principles I work to: the code of conduct of CIISec, through my membership; the ACPO principles for digital evidence; and, as an expert witness, my overriding duty to the court. I am responsible for applying them in my own work and in the investigations I lead.
D2.action: I judged that verbal permission was insufficient: accessing an account without the owner's authority risks an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990. Before proceeding, I obtained written authorisation from both the client and the account owner and confirmed the legal basis for access. The same principles govern all of my work: acting in the public and organisational interest; reporting accurately and objectively, clearly distinguishing fact from assumption; protecting confidentiality, including how and where data is stored and encrypted; accessing only the data an investigation requires, consistent with the data minimisation principle of the UK GDPR; never exceeding authorised access; working within my competence and engaging specialists where needed; avoiding conflicts of interest; and maintaining an audit trail of my actions and rationale.
D2.result: I accessed the mailbox only once written authorisation and the legal basis were confirmed, so the evidence could be relied upon in court. I subsequently gave expert evidence in the Malaysian court, and the client's claim succeeded.
D2.followup: My audit trail for each investigation also informs the lessons-learned review that follows.

D3.situation: Incident response frequently involves legal and regulatory obligations under time pressure. In a multinational ransomware response, the client faced notification obligations to regulators in several jurisdictions, and any engagement with the threat actor carried sanctions risk. In a separate civil matter, my forensic work had to be lawful and admissible before a Malaysian court.
D3.task: I was responsible for ensuring that my own and my team's work complied with these requirements, and for supporting clients in meeting theirs. Decisions on notification and payment rested with the clients and their legal advisers.
D3.action: In the ransomware response, I ensured all updates were provided under legal privilege, supported the client's notifications to regulators, including the ICO under the 72-hour requirement in Article 33 of the UK GDPR, and ensured sanctions screening was completed before any engagement with the threat actor. In the litigation matter, I examined cloud storage and email only under the authority of a court order, in accordance with the ACPO principles and ISO/IEC 27037:2012. In policing, I examined locked devices using specialist tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite, always under the appropriate legal authority. My work also takes account of the Data Protection Act 2018, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the Investigatory Powers Act 2016.
D3.result: The sanctions checks confirmed that engagement could proceed lawfully. In the litigation matter, I provided an affidavit and gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the client's claim succeeded.
D3.followup: I follow a structured process built on authoritative sources: NCSC and ICO alerts and guidance, professional events and communities, and forthcoming legislation such as the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which will update the NIS Regulations 2018. Much of my current work is with CNI organisations, and this informs the UK forensic laboratory I am building, so that clients can comply with new requirements from the outset.

D4.situation: Clients, insurers and courts expect incident response to follow recognised standards. As DFIR lead, I determine which standards apply to my team's work and to the plans I deliver for clients.
D4.task: I am responsible for identifying the standards relevant to my team's services and implementing them, both in our own accreditations and in client work.
D4.action: In my first year as DFIR lead, I achieved ISO/IEC 27001, the NCSC CIR scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials, designing our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset. When a managed service client's incident response plan (IRP) was outdated, I aligned the replacement to the NIST SP 800-61r3 lifecycle and ISO/IEC 27035, and mapped six runbooks to MITRE ATT&CK. In forensic examinations, I apply the ACPO principles and ISO/IEC 27037:2012 for evidence handling.
D4.result: The team passed all three accreditation assessments at the first attempt. The client formally approved the new IRP and adopted it as the standard for its SOC and incident response teams.
D4.followup: The client's IRP is subject to annual review, with additional reviews following significant vendor or network changes. I also maintain our methodology documents, which provide repeatable approaches for Windows, Linux and Mac forensics and for AWS, GCP and Azure, aligned to NIST and SANS frameworks. I update them to reflect changes in attacker TTPs, including the growing use of AI in attacks.

E1.situation: Digital forensics, incident response and threat intelligence evolve rapidly, with attacker TTPs and investigative tooling changing constantly, increasingly driven by AI. Protecting CNI and OT is a fast-moving, specialised field in which threats can rapidly escalate into critical incidents.
E1.task: I am responsible for maintaining current knowledge of DFIR and CTI, and for recording my CPD in support of my certifications and professional memberships.
E1.action: I attend a deliberate mix of conferences: Black Hat, for the past three years, for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability; Infosecurity Europe for the wider market and governance landscape; and BSides for practitioner-led content and peer engagement. To develop my OT capability, I completed the two-day OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp, covering CNI protection, OT and ICS security, and threat prevention. Earlier, in policing, I completed training in Android debugging and used specialist mobile forensic tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite to examine locked devices. Alongside formal learning, I review industry news, research and regulatory developments daily.
E1.result: I achieved the OPSWAT certification for the MetaDefender platform. I target 20 to 40 hours of formal CPD each year from training and conferences, recorded in my SANS account towards renewal of my GCFA certification, which GIAC reviews at each renewal.
E1.followup: I will attend Black Hat and BSides London in December 2026, and the GCFA renewal requirement ensures that my CPD remains recorded and on track each year.

E2.situation: DFIR and intelligence work often takes place in isolated or air-gapped environments, or on client sites without approved tooling. Commercial and open-source tools are fragmented, sit behind paywalls or operate as cloud services to which sensitive data cannot be uploaded.
E2.task: I chose to contribute to the profession by building and sharing free tools, and to promote it by sharing knowledge publicly. These are personal projects for which I am solely responsible.
E2.action: I designed and built a suite of more than 40 free, open-source tools that run entirely in the browser, with development accelerated by AI. They span the incident lifecycle, from case management, email header and PowerShell analysis to file hashing, and include MITRE ATT&CK mapping and assessment tools based on the NCSC CAF. I also built fx, a graphical forensic triage tool that parses Windows host artefacts, hashes all evidence and automatically hunts for the TTPs and IOCs of prolific ransomware groups, with findings mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. Following the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024, I published newly registered CrowdStrike-themed domains daily on X and LinkedIn for defenders to block. I discussed AI, DFIR and cyber resilience on the Richmond Advisory Group's Cyber Sidekicks podcast in October 2025 and contributed to coverage in the Daily Mail and on Times Radio. In policing, I presented to the Bedford branch of BCS and lectured colleagues on the dark web, cyber crime and digital currencies.
E2.result: Both projects are publicly available on GitHub, and fx, at version 0.1.4, has been used on live investigations by me and other practitioners. Named industry practitioners testing fx have given positive feedback on its ability to identify malicious activity and have suggested future enhancements.
E2.followup: fx remains under active development, and I use this feedback to shape its roadmap.

E3.situation: As DFIR lead, I recognised that, without an intelligence capability, my team was limited in its ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour and advise clients beyond the immediate incident. Clients were also increasingly seeking a service that combined reactive and proactive support. I had built a comparable service in my previous role, where it generated 15% of total incident response revenue across reactive work and retainers.
E3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a threat intelligence offering with two objectives: strengthening our incident response with timely intelligence, and establishing a standalone service with a clear market differentiator.
E3.action: I structured the workstream around the intelligence lifecycle, from direction and collection through analysis and dissemination, and evaluated several commercial intelligence products to complement the team's own dark web persona footprint, capability and open-source tooling. Beyond monitoring each client's own exposure, the service mapped critical suppliers through stakeholder interviews and monitored them for indicators of risk, for example a supplier with 50 infostealer infections in the past month, or a supplier holding client data that had suffered a ransomware attack. This enabled clients to understand and act on supply chain risk, in line with NCSC supply chain security guidance. I launched the service in partnership with the marketing team.
E3.result: Intelligence rapidly became integral to our incident response process: from the outset, the team gathered current TTPs, IOCs and campaign intelligence to support engagements, accelerating the detection of malicious activity. Client feedback on the launch was positive, and supply chain coverage was a key factor in its success, particularly as the launch coincided with several high-profile ransomware incidents enabled by supply chain compromise.
E3.followup: I share intelligence with the wider community through a threat intelligence webinar, open to all, which has grown without advertising to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries. Following attendee feedback, it now runs quarterly with a sector focus.
